\section*{Limitations}

\paragraph{Constraint scope.}
CF is an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement: CF$\leftrightarrow$DR represents a fundamental trade-off (eliminating CF re-routes violations to DR; Appendix~\ref{app:cf-dr-tradeoff}), and its impact is model-dependent (S1 introduces CF for calibrated models but reduces it for poorly-calibrated ones).
Global entity-level type consensus during decoding offers the most direct path to resolving CF.
Entity-first generation order is an architectural constraint: the grammar enforces entities before relations, ensuring the registry is populated before type checks; alternative orderings would require deferred constraint evaluation.
Residual DR under fine-tuning (36 violations total) decomposes into entity type errors (39\%), schema coverage gaps (33\%), and model generation errors (28\%); schema gaps arise from training-data-derived constraints that may not cover all valid type pairs (Appendix~\ref{app:residual-dr-analysis}).
Our empirical constraints are derived from training data type-pair co-occurrences; schema evolution (adding new entity types or relations) would require constraint regeneration, and the 0.6--1.0\% uncovered valid type pairs suggest potential over-restriction during transition periods.
We do not decompose CF violations into first-seen cascading errors versus legitimate type ambiguity; this decomposition requires gold entity type annotations at the mention level, which SciERC provides only at the entity level.
Post-hoc type consensus re-voting eliminates all CF in our experiments, at the cost of DR regression (up to $+$9.38\,pp on DocRED zero-shot; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}); integrating consensus into the decoding loop remains future work.

\paragraph{Evaluation coverage.}
Zero-shot evaluation covers three 8B-class and one 70B-class model; fine-tuning composability is validated on two 8B-class models (full datasets) and one 70B-class model (SciERC full, DocRED 200-document subset).
Scaling to smaller models has not been verified; the schema restrictiveness--enforcement difficulty relationship is based on three schemas.
Evaluation is limited to one fine-tuning method (LoRA); LoRA hyperparameters were tuned on SciERC and transferred to DocRED without dataset-specific optimization, which may underestimate DocRED potential.
WikiEvents fine-tuning is preliminary ($n{=}20$); DocRED uses the development set (test annotations unavailable).
All main experiments use greedy decoding; beam search compatibility is confirmed but comprehensive evaluation across all configurations remains future work (Appendices~\ref{app:sampling},~\ref{app:beam-search}).

\paragraph{Engineering considerations.}
Our approach requires access to model logits, excluding API-only models; continuation masking assumes distinguishable token prefixes per type name, which may be challenged by morphologically similar types (e.g., \texttt{Protein} vs.\ \texttt{Protein\_Complex}; Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).
70B experiments use AWQ INT4 quantization; an 8B ablation confirms enforcement is unaffected (Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}), though a direct 70B FP16 comparison exceeds our hardware capacity.
Evaluation is limited to English-language datasets; the mechanism is language-independent but CJK tokenization fragmentation may increase masking steps (Appendix~\ref{app:scalability}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.

Existing grammar-constrained decoding frameworks (e.g., XGrammar) enforce level~1 constraints---structural validity and vocabulary membership---but IE domain/range rules require cross-position entity-type state that context-free grammars cannot express.
We formalize this gap:

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Proposition 1} (Level 2 $\not\subseteq$ Level 1)\textbf{.}
\textit{Domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets are not context-free.}

\smallskip
\noindent\textit{Proof sketch.}
An output contains $n$ entities with independently chosen types, followed by a relation referencing head $e_k$ for arbitrary $k \leq n$.
A PDA's LIFO stack cannot retrieve position $k$ without destroying entries above it; since both $n$ and $k$ are unbounded, no PDA can enforce this constraint (formal pumping argument in Appendix~\ref{app:pumping-lemma}).
OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map enabling random-access type lookups).\hfill$\square$

\smallskip
The proof establishes theoretical impossibility for unbounded entity sets; the following paragraph addresses the finite (practical) case.

\paragraph{Engineering applicability.}
When the entity set is finite, the valid language is technically regular, but the corresponding DFA requires $O(|\mathcal{E}|^{|\text{entities}|})$ states.
For typical SciERC documents (median 17 entities, 6 types), a DFA would require $6^{17} \approx 1.6{\times}10^{13}$ states; for DocRED (median 19 entities, 6 types), $6^{19} \approx 6.1{\times}10^{14}$ states---well beyond practical construction for online decoding.
The exponential scaling makes pure-grammar enforcement impractical for all but the smallest documents; OntoCoDec's registry-based approach avoids both the theoretical impossibility (unbounded) and the engineering intractability (finite but exponential).

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 3 datasets, 3+ models, and 2 tasks.
Because IE type constraints exceed context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), the semantic layer bridges the gap grammar-only enforcement cannot address (3\% vs.\ 94\% DR reduction at 8B), using constructive forward masking over a dynamic entity registry.
This scale-dependent interaction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results})---likely reflecting improved vocabulary calibration at larger scale, where 70B models assign higher probability to ontology-valid tokens (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing})---suggests grammar-constrained decoding is necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

4	\section{Full Proof of Proposition 1}
5	\label{app:pumping-lemma}
6	
7	We prove that domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets cannot be expressed by any context-free grammar, using the pumping lemma for context-free languages.
8	
9	\begin{proof}
10	Define the language $L$ of valid IE outputs over ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ with $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, $\mathcal{R} = \{r\}$, and $\sigma(r) = \{(\tau_A, \tau_A)\}$ (i.e., $r$ requires both head and tail to be type $\tau_A$).
11	
12	An output string has the form:
13	\[
14	w = e_1\, e_2\, \cdots\, e_n\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_k,\, r,\, \tau^h)
15	\]
16	where each $e_i$ is an entity with type $\tau_{a_i} \in \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, and $\tau^h$ is the head type field of a relation triple referencing entity $e_k$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$).
17	
18	The type-validity constraint requires $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k}$ (the head type must match the referenced entity's type) \emph{and} $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
19	Combined: a string $w \in L$ if and only if $\tau_{a_k} = \tau_A$.
20	
21	Now consider strings of the specific form:
22	\[
23	w_n = \underbrace{\tau_B\; \tau_B\; \cdots\; \tau_B}_{n-1}\; \tau_A\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_n,\, r,\, \tau_A)
24	\]
25	where the first $n{-}1$ entities have type $\tau_B$ and only entity $e_n$ has type $\tau_A$.
26	The relation references $e_n$, so $\tau^h = \tau_A = \tau_{a_n}$, satisfying both the registry consistency and domain constraint.
27	Thus $w_n \in L$ for all $n$.
28	
29	Assume for contradiction that $L$ is context-free.
30	By the pumping lemma, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ where:
31	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
32	    \item $|vy| \geq 1$,
33	    \item $|vxy| \leq p$,
34	    \item $uv^i xy^i z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
35	\end{enumerate}
36	
37	Choose $w = w_n$ with $n > p$.

\section{Full Proof of Proposition 1}
\label{app:pumping-lemma}

We prove that domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets cannot be expressed by any context-free grammar, using the pumping lemma for context-free languages.

\begin{proof}
Define the language $L$ of valid IE outputs over ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ with $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, $\mathcal{R} = \{r\}$, and $\sigma(r) = \{(\tau_A, \tau_A)\}$ (i.e., $r$ requires both head and tail to be type $\tau_A$).

An output string has the form:
\[
w = e_1\, e_2\, \cdots\, e_n\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_k,\, r,\, \tau^h)
\]
where each $e_i$ is an entity with type $\tau_{a_i} \in \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, and $\tau^h$ is the head type field of a relation triple referencing entity $e_k$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$).

The type-validity constraint requires $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k}$ (the head type must match the referenced entity's type) \emph{and} $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
Combined: a string $w \in L$ if and only if $\tau_{a_k} = \tau_A$.

Now consider strings of the specific form:
\[
w_n = \underbrace{\tau_B\; \tau_B\; \cdots\; \tau_B}_{n-1}\; \tau_A\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_n,\, r,\, \tau_A)
\]
where the first $n{-}1$ entities have type $\tau_B$ and only entity $e_n$ has type $\tau_A$.
The relation references $e_n$, so $\tau^h = \tau_A = \tau_{a_n}$, satisfying both the registry consistency and domain constraint.
Thus $w_n \in L$ for all $n$.

Assume for contradiction that $L$ is context-free.
By the pumping lemma, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $|vy| \geq 1$,
    \item $|vxy| \leq p$,
    \item $uv^i xy^i z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
\end{enumerate}

Choose $w = w_n$ with $n > p$.
The entity list portion $\tau_B^{n-1}\, \tau_A$ has length $n > p$, so the pumpable region $vxy$ (with $|vxy| \leq p$) must lie entirely within the entity list (it cannot span from the entity list to the relation reference, which is separated by $n - p > 0$ entity tokens from the start).

\textbf{Case 1:} $v$ or $y$ contains entity tokens from the $\tau_B^{n-1}$ prefix.
Pumping up ($i = 2$): $uv^2 xy^2 z$ inserts additional $\tau_B$ entities, increasing $n$ to some $n' > n$.
But the relation reference still points to entity $e_n$ (at the original position), which is now at a different position in the longer entity list.
The entity at position $n$ in the pumped string is $\tau_B$ (since we inserted $\tau_B$ tokens before position $n$, shifting $\tau_A$ to position $n' > n$).
Thus $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B = \tau_{a_n'}$, where $n'$ is the new position of entity $e_n$.
More precisely: the relation references a fixed entity name $e_k$, but pumping changes the entity-type binding at that name's position.
Since the pumped string assigns $\tau_B$ at position $k$ (which originally had $\tau_A$), the type-validity constraint $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k} \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ is violated.
Hence $uv^2 xy^2 z \notin L$, contradicting condition (iii).

\textbf{Case 2:} $v$ or $y$ contains the $\tau_A$ token at position $n$.
Pumping down ($i = 0$): $uxz$ removes the only $\tau_A$ entity.
The relation's head entity reference now points to a position that either does not exist or has type $\tau_B$.
In either case, $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B$, violating type validity.
Hence $uxz \notin L$, contradicting condition (iii).

In both cases, the pumping lemma is violated, so $L$ is not context-free.
The key insight is that type-validity requires a \emph{binding} between an entity's type (assigned at an earlier position) and the relation's type field (at a later position), with the binding target determined by the entity name.
Pumping disrupts this binding by changing which entity occupies a given position, while the relation reference remains fixed---a cross-position dependency that pushdown automata cannot track with their LIFO stack discipline.

OntoCoDec's semantic layer addresses this with a runtime entity registry $\mathcal{D}$ (a finite map), operating as a deterministic stateful transducer that provides random-access type lookups, beyond the expressive power of context-free grammars.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Finite entity sets.}
For a finite entity set $\mathcal{E}$ with canonical identifiers, the valid language $L_{\text{valid}} = \bigcap_i L_i$ is theoretically regular (a finite intersection of regular languages).
However, the corresponding DFA requires $O(|\mathcal{T}|^{|\mathcal{E}|})$ states---for SciERC with 6 entity types and typical documents containing 20+ entities, this exceeds $10^{15}$ states, rendering explicit construction impractical.
Moreover, real IE operates over open-vocabulary text spans rather than closed identifier sets, making the general (non-regular) formulation the appropriate model.
Proposition~1 motivates the runtime state-tracking architecture for this general case.

\paragraph{Position indexing vs.\ name referencing.}
The proof above uses position-based entity indexing ($e_k$ at position $k$) for expository clarity.
In OntoCoDec's actual JSON output, relation triples reference entities by name strings rather than positional indices.
The core argument transfers directly: validating type consistency requires a name$\to$type lookup over dynamically generated bindings, which is a random-access map operation.
A PDA's LIFO stack cannot perform random-access retrieval by key (it can only inspect the top element), so the non-context-free result holds regardless of whether entities are referenced by position or by name.
Name-based referencing strictly subsumes position-based indexing: any position-based constraint can be expressed via names (assign names $e_1, \ldots, e_n$ in order), but name-based constraints additionally permit cross-field coreference (the same entity name appearing in multiple triples must carry the same type), which position indexing cannot express.
Thus, the position-based formulation is a simplification that makes the pumping argument more transparent without weakening the conclusion.

9	OntoCoDec applies constructive forward masking via a dynamic entity registry, enforcing schema semantics within a single forward pass.
10	
11	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
12	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, and others~\cite{guidex2025,josifoski2022genie,paolini2021tanl,cabot2021rebel,wang2023instructuie,qi2024adelie,fei2022lasuie,lu2022uie,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure via training-time internalization without runtime enforcement~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with a preliminary event extraction pilot (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We hypothesize this reflects improved vocabulary calibration: larger models assign higher probability to ontology-valid tokens, reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates follow an observed pattern consistent with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering discards up to 74\% of predictions including true positives (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with a scale-dependent layer interaction: at 8B, the semantic layer achieves only 24\% independent DR reduction (near-complete when combined), while at 70B it reaches 84\% independently.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 reduces DR to near-zero: DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\% at R-F1 40--46\% ($\pm$0.3\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types at 8B on both RE datasets under fine-tuning (1.39$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% on SciERC and 42--90\% on DocRED, with total violations decreasing $\sim$31\% (Appendix~\ref{app:cross-model-zs}).

OntoCoDec is a constraint enforcement method, orthogonal and complementary to training-based schema-aware approaches such as GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie} and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}; it can be composed with any generative IE system to improve schema compliance without retraining.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item Systematic ablation across 3 model families (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) and 2 datasets (SciERC, DocRED) under both zero-shot and LoRA fine-tuned settings, demonstrating DR reduction to $\leq$0.21\% with R-F1 within $\pm$0.3\,pp; DR enforcement introduces CF as a correctable side effect (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}).
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework grounded in the observation that domain/range type constraints require stateful enforcement beyond context-free grammars---grammar-only approaches face state spaces of $6^{17}$--$6^{19}$ for typical IE schemas (Proposition~1; \S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas with up to 96 relation types.
    \item Preliminary single-family scale exploration on Llama-3.1-70B (AWQ INT4), revealing a scale-dependent layer interaction: the semantic layer alone achieves 84\% DR reduction at 70B vs.\ 24\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}). At 8B, beam $k{=}2$ is Pareto-optimal (R-F1 44.60, CF 0.11\%, 1.18$\times$ greedy S1 latency); $k{=}4$ achieves DR${=}$0\% with near-zero CF at 1.39$\times$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Full Proof of Proposition 1}
\label{app:pumping-lemma}

We prove that domain/range type constraints for IE with unbounded entity sets cannot be expressed by any context-free grammar, using the pumping lemma for context-free languages.

\begin{proof}
Define the language $L$ of valid IE outputs over ontology $\mathcal{O} = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \sigma)$ with $\mathcal{E} = \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, $\mathcal{R} = \{r\}$, and $\sigma(r) = \{(\tau_A, \tau_A)\}$ (i.e., $r$ requires both head and tail to be type $\tau_A$).

An output string has the form:
\[
w = e_1\, e_2\, \cdots\, e_n\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_k,\, r,\, \tau^h)
\]
where each $e_i$ is an entity with type $\tau_{a_i} \in \{\tau_A, \tau_B\}$, and $\tau^h$ is the head type field of a relation triple referencing entity $e_k$ ($1 \leq k \leq n$).

The type-validity constraint requires $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k}$ (the head type must match the referenced entity's type) \emph{and} $\tau^h \in \operatorname{dom}(r) = \{\tau_A\}$.
Combined: a string $w \in L$ if and only if $\tau_{a_k} = \tau_A$.

Now consider strings of the specific form:
\[
w_n = \underbrace{\tau_B\; \tau_B\; \cdots\; \tau_B}_{n-1}\; \tau_A\;\; \texttt{REL}(h{=}e_n,\, r,\, \tau_A)
\]
where the first $n{-}1$ entities have type $\tau_B$ and only entity $e_n$ has type $\tau_A$.
The relation references $e_n$, so $\tau^h = \tau_A = \tau_{a_n}$, satisfying both the registry consistency and domain constraint.
Thus $w_n \in L$ for all $n$.

Assume for contradiction that $L$ is context-free.
By the pumping lemma, there exists a pumping length $p$ such that any $w \in L$ with $|w| \geq p$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ where:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $|vy| \geq 1$,
    \item $|vxy| \leq p$,
    \item $uv^i xy^i z \in L$ for all $i \geq 0$.
\end{enumerate}

Choose $w = w_n$ with $n > p$.
The entity list portion $\tau_B^{n-1}\, \tau_A$ has length $n > p$, so the pumpable region $vxy$ (with $|vxy| \leq p$) must lie entirely within the entity list (it cannot span from the entity list to the relation reference, which is separated by $n - p > 0$ entity tokens from the start).

\textbf{Case 1:} $v$ or $y$ contains entity tokens from the $\tau_B^{n-1}$ prefix.
Pumping up ($i = 2$): $uv^2 xy^2 z$ inserts additional $\tau_B$ entities, increasing $n$ to some $n' > n$.
But the relation reference still points to entity $e_n$ (at the original position), which is now at a different position in the longer entity list.
The entity at position $n$ in the pumped string is $\tau_B$ (since we inserted $\tau_B$ tokens before position $n$, shifting $\tau_A$ to position $n' > n$).
Thus $\tau^h = \tau_A \neq \tau_B = \tau_{a_n'}$, where $n'$ is the new position of entity $e_n$.
More precisely: the relation references a fixed entity name $e_k$, but pumping changes the entity-type binding at that name's position.
Since the pumped string assigns $\tau_B$ at position $k$ (which originally had $\tau_A$), the type-validity constraint $\tau^h = \tau_{a_k} \in \operatorname{dom}(r)$ is violated.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with a preliminary event extraction pilot (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.

\begin{abstract}
Large language models for information extraction generate structurally valid but ontologically invalid triples---where entity types violate the ontology's domain/range constraints.
These violations persist across the capability spectrum and cannot be addressed by grammar-constrained decoding (which lacks cross-field type awareness) or post-hoc filtering (which discards valid predictions).

A decidability analysis shows that domain/range constraints exceed context-free expressiveness, yielding a two-layer architecture: a grammar layer enforces structural validity and vocabulary membership; a semantic layer enforces type constraints at runtime through stateful masking over a dynamic entity registry.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion

OntoCoDec compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints, validated across 2 RE datasets (SciERC, DocRED) and 3 model families, with a preliminary event extraction pilot (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
The central empirical finding is non-additive layer interaction: grammar alone achieves 3\% DR reduction on SciERC, semantic alone 24\%, but their composition yields 94\% at 8B (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results})---an enabling dependency where grammar-enforced vocabulary membership creates the clean input the semantic layer requires.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent layer interaction.}
This dependency weakens at scale: at 70B, the semantic layer independently achieves 84\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
We offer a speculative hypothesis: larger models exhibit improved vocabulary calibration, assigning higher probability to ontology-valid tokens and reducing the semantic layer's dependence on grammar-enforced vocabulary membership (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}); confirming this causal mechanism requires cross-family verification beyond our current scope.
Supporting evidence includes the fallback frequency gap: under LoRA + S1, Qwen-8B triggers 0 grammar-first fallbacks on SciERC while Llama-8B triggers 5{,}882 (Table~\ref{tab:ft-ablation}), yet both achieve DR\,$\leq$\,0.21\%, confirming that fallback frequency does not determine enforcement effectiveness.
Grammar-constrained decoding is thus necessary but increasingly insufficient as models improve; constraint enforcement is preserved under INT4 quantization (4$\times$ compression; Appendix~\ref{app:quantization}).

\paragraph{DR$\leftrightarrow$CF trade-off.}
Greedy S1 reduces DR to $\leq$\,0.21\% but introduces CF (zero-shot $+$9.82\,pp, fine-tuned $+$1.18\,pp)---an architectural consequence of per-triple independent enforcement.
Among 248 zero-shot CF violations, 58.1\% involve hallucinated entities (absent from gold) and only 7.3\% are true cascade errors (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); fine-tuned CF drops to $\leq$1.4\%.
Beam $k{=}2$ reduces CF to 0.11\% at 1.18$\times$ latency (Pareto-optimal; recommended for zero-shot deployment); $k{=}4$ eliminates all violations at 8B (1 residual CF at 70B) at 1.39$\times$ (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Net effect: total violations decrease ${\sim}$31\% in zero-shot and ${>}$90\% under fine-tuning; DR is irrecoverable while CF is amenable to post-hoc resolution (TCR; Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).

\paragraph{Complementarity and deployment.}
GoLLIE and KnowCoder internalize schema knowledge via training but lack runtime guarantees; LoRA + S1 shows the two are complementary (DR 1--2\%\,$\to$\,$\leq$0.21\%; neither alone achieves both high R-F1 and near-zero DR).
S2 (two-pass) exhibits scale-sensitive behavior: comparable to S1 at 8B but $-$8\,pp R-F1 at 70B, consistent with CRANE's~\cite{banerjee2025crane} finding that aggressive constraint enforcement can interfere with well-calibrated reasoning; we recommend S1 as the default configuration.

\paragraph{Per-triple vs.\ global enforcement.}
Per-triple enforcement cannot coordinate cross-triple type assignments---the source of CF (Level~3; \S\ref{sec:decidability}); global entity-level type consensus exceeds online per-token masking.
Beam search and TCR approximate this; integrating consensus into decoding remains future work.
